opener.heading: Week 32: Sports & Team Play ⚽
about: This week Azlyn builds a sport out of its parts. A ball wound from grocery bags on Friday, a numbered shirt on Saturday, a whistle and three signals on Sunday, five events chalked onto the path on Monday, a long jump measured in string on Tuesday, half-time drinks she mixes to her own recipe on Wednesday. The question sitting under all of it: what does a game need before anybody can play it? On Thursday she answers it by making up a game of her own and running the whole thing end to end.

Nothing lands in this week but the heat, and it shapes every day. The outdoor hour goes before eleven, and the afternoon event sits indoors at a table, on the floor or on a tray. Four things get built to be used later: Friday's wound ball, Saturday's numbered shirts, Sunday's peg scoreboard and Monday's five chalked stations all come back out on Thursday. Keep the first three somewhere she can see them, because the week ends with a trophy and she needs to know what it is for.
azlyn: Sorting by what a thing does. Balls go in the HIGH basket or the LOW one, and only dropping them settles which.
Stopping on a signal. One whistle blast freezes her mid-stride, two turn her round, three put everybody on the floor.
Measuring with string. A cut length holds a jump, so three jumps lie side by side on the wall and she sorts them longest to shortest.
Keeping a score. One point, one peg, one space along the line, counted out loud.
Writing rules and mending them. She invents a game, plays it until something breaks, and says what the new rule should be.
you: Sorting by an invisible property is a step up
Oil and water is the same lesson as the wax crayon and the sticker resist
Freezing on cue is one of the best self-control exercises there is
Choosing what to leave out is harder than choosing what to include
Sand is one of the best materials there is, and it's the resistance that makes it good
"Too much" and "not enough" is a real concept, and it's rarely taught
Asking for her rule is better than checking her answer
shopping: Every ball in the house, 8–12 (soccer ball, tennis ball, ping-pong ball)
Clean socks, 1 pair, and 1 old sock you won't want back
Thick card, 5 sheets, or flattened boxes (one sheet is August's handprints)
A pair of adult scissors (adult only)
A sharp knife and a board (adult only)
Chalk, enough for two pairs of hands
Jam jars, 4, one of them with a lid
Food coloring, or a drop of the paint
A white wax crayon, or a white candle stub
Washable poster paint in two colors (fabric paint if you have it)
A washcloth you can wet, for the handprint sheet
1 pencil, if you are marking the door frame this month
A sponge, or a stiff brush
Flattened cardboard, one piece per shirt
A cereal box, and 4 blank cards
A shoebox with a lid, and a small box with a lid
Washed play sand, 1 bag (not construction sand)
A large shallow storage tub, or the paddling pool
Frozen juice concentrate, or lemons and sugar
Ice, and the ice tray filled the night before
opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 14 months this week. He scribbles with his whole fist, stacks two blocks, and has three to five words you can make out. He also walks into the middle of whatever is going on, which is why the small balls, the bottle caps and the whistle get counted into a box and stood up high at the end of every day.

days.title: The Bounce Test
days.prepTonight: Send a laundry basket round the house tonight for every ball in it, and leave an orange, clean socks and a sheet of foil beside it.

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Ball Made of Bags and String

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: The Forks and the Water Pitcher

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Cool Bath and the Soccer Book

opening.title: Rounding Up the Balls
opening.need: 1 laundry basket · every ball in the house · 1 orange · 1 pair of clean socks · 1 sheet of kitchen foil.
steps: Hand her the basket and send her round the house. Under the beds, the closet, the shed shelf. Eight is enough, twelve is better.
Add three things that are not balls. Roll the socks into one, scrunch the foil into another, put the orange on top.
Line them up in the order she thinks they bounce, best to worst. You test that order at quarter past nine.

main.title: High Bouncer, Low Bouncer
materials: Every ball in the house, 8–12 (soccer ball, tennis ball, ping-pong ball, the sock ball, the orange, this morning's foil ball)
4 sheets of paper for her predictions
A clear stretch of hard floor and a wall
steps: Tape a strip to the wall at your shoulder height and write DROP HERE on it. Every ball starts against that tape and gets let go, never thrown.
Stand the two baskets a stride back on either side. Tape a label on each, HIGH and LOW.
Drop the first ball. Watch where the top of the bounce reaches on her, knee or waist or shoulder. She calls it.
Before each new ball she squeezes it and says which basket it lands in. Write the prediction down and tick it after the drop.
Work through the lot on hard floor. The orange divides opinion and the foil ball disappoints her.
Count each basket and read the prediction sheet back, ticks and all. Ask what the high ones have in common and write her answer word for word.
main.tip: The squeeze is doing the work. Hard and springy comes back, soft and dead does not.

outside.title: Where the Ball Bounces Best
paras: Take the tennis ball and a piece of chalk to the front and bounce it on everything hard enough to bounce on. The paving, the drain cover, the driveway, the grass baked flat since June. Chalk an H or an L on each as she calls it, and finish on the shaded lawn, which still has give in it.

days.infant: Kreston is 14 months and walks into the middle of whatever is happening. Give him the soccer ball, the one ball too big to fit in his mouth, and sit a few feet off with your legs open. Roll it across and wait. He shoves it back with both hands.

second.title: The Ball Made of Bags and String
second.intro: Children in half the world make their own soccer balls, and this is how.
materials: 1 ball of string or thick wool
The taped mark on the wall from this morning
steps: Scrunch two sheets of newspaper into the tightest ball she can manage. Squeeze, do not fold. That lump sets the size of everything after it.
Push the core into the old sock, knot it tight above, and cut the tail off with your scissors.
Wrap a grocery bag round the sock and twist the handles down flat. Then the next over the twist from a different side, four to six in all.
Hold the bundle while she winds the string. Round, then across, then round again. Twenty turns leaves an egg. Fifty looks like a ball.
Tie the string off, cover the knot with packing tape, and run masking tape over any bag still showing.
Take it to the taped mark on the wall. She calls high or low, then drops it, and finds she was right about a sock ball.
Out on the grass, kick it. It flies heavy and dead and will not roll far, which is what makes it good on a dry lawn.
second.tip: Wind the string tighter than feels reasonable. A loose ball goes egg-shaped on the second kick, and the fix is another fifty turns.

alternatives: Sock ball only. Roll two socks into each other and stop there.
Wind string round a tennis ball you own and compare the two.
Sort the morning's balls by size instead of bounce.
outAgain: A café with a window seat, cake and an hour of watching people go past
The shady half of the park, once the paving is off the boil
The playing field at the end of the road, with the new ball
Home and the hose, if the heat has beaten everyone

aroundWorld.title: The World's Game ⚽
paras: More people play soccer than any other game on earth, and most of them never owned a store-bought ball. In Ghana, Brazil and the Philippines children wind grocery bags, rags and string into one the same way Azlyn did this afternoon, and no two of them come out alike.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Half-time oranges, the way teams everywhere have taken them for a hundred years. Cut two into six wedges each and hand them round at the halfway point of whatever game she plays this week.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: In Brazil a ball wound out of rags is a bola de meia, which means sock ball.

days.krestonPM: Give him a sheet of the newspaper to scrunch and tear while you wind, and keep the grocery bags up on the table. At 14 months the noise is half the appeal. Hand him the finished ball first. It takes both arms.

insight.headline: Sorting by an invisible property is a step up.
paras: Azlyn has sorted by color, shape and size since she was two, and all three sit on the surface of the object. Bounce hides until you drop it. To put a ball in the right basket she has to hold a category the ball's appearance does not hand her, then find the evidence herself. Researchers watch for this shift around three, sorting by what a thing does rather than what it looks like. The squeeze test is the bigger move, because she is predicting an outcome from a feel. She will be wrong about the orange. Being wrong out loud and then watching is what makes the rule stick.

days.safety: Ping-pong balls and anything smaller than a tennis ball fit down Kreston's throat, and at 14 months he walks into the middle of things to get at them. Count the small ones into the basket at the end and stand it up high. The bouncing out front stops at the curb: hold his hand from the curb onward, keep the drain cover on your side of him, and any ball that gets away is yours to fetch, never hers. August sun burns faster than it feels, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. The scissors stay with you.

days.title: Team Colors
days.prepTonight: Water two colors of poster paint down into jam jars, stand them on the table with the white wax crayon, and dig out three or four old white t-shirts.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: Oil, Water and a Good Shake

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Number the Paint Runs Off

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: Ten Kicks Against the Shed Wall

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Numbers Laid Out on the Floor

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Bath, and Her Shirt Laid Out for Tomorrow

opening.title: Oil, Water and a Good Shake
opening.need: 1 clear jar with a lid · water · 2 tablespoons cooking oil · 1 tablespoon · a drop of food coloring or watered paint.
steps: Half fill the jar with water and let her stir a drop of color through it.
Pour in two tablespoons of oil, lid on tight, and let her shake it as hard as she can.
Stand it on the table and watch. The oil climbs back to the top every time. Tell her a crayon does the same trick at quarter past nine.

main.title: The Number the Paint Runs Off
materials: 1 white wax crayon or a white candle stub
Washable poster paint in two colors, watered down in jam jars
steps: She picks the team's two colors out of the jars and names the team. Write the name on the back of one sheet in marker.
Give her the white crayon and a sheet of thick paper. She draws a big number, pressing hard. It comes out close to invisible.
Load the wide brush with the first watery color and wash it edge to edge in one direction. The number rises up through it.
Rinse the brush in the jar of clean water and dry it on the towel before the second color, or you get mud.
Do a second sheet in the other color, and a third with a stripe of each meeting in the middle.
Hand her the last three sheets to do on her own. Write a squad number on the back of each and lay them out of the sun to dry.
main.tip: Press hard with the crayon and water the paint down further than looks sensible. Thick paint covers the wax instead of sliding off it.

outside.title: Ten Kicks Against the Shed Wall
paras: Chalk a rectangle on the shed door at her height and get out at half past ten, while the shed wall still throws shade onto the paving. Ten kicks each, counted out loud, and a chalk tally on the paving for every one that lands inside the box. Leave the tally where it is. Tomorrow needs a scoreboard.

days.infant: Kreston is 14 months and scribbling, so hand him a fat piece of chalk and let him work the paving beside the tally marks. He holds it in his fist and drags it, and every line on there is his. He will walk into the goal about six times.

second.title: Numbers on Real Shirts
second.intro: The wax trick works on cloth too, and this one comes off the line in time for tomorrow.
materials: 3–4 old white t-shirts (pillowcases work if you have no spare shirts)
Washable poster paint or fabric paint
Flattened cardboard, one piece per shirt
1 sheet of thick card for the August handprints
1 wide soft brush, from this morning
1 pencil, if you are marking the door frame this month
steps: Slide a piece of cardboard inside each shirt, up to the shoulders. Paint goes through cotton in seconds and the card is the only thing stopping it.
Tear the masking tape into strips and build a number on the back of the first shirt. Straight lines only. A 1 is one strip, a 7 is two, a 4 is three. Press every edge down hard.
Let her build the next number herself. Crooked is correct. If she wants a 12, both digits go on.
Load the sponge and press it straight down over the tape rather than brushing across. Brushing lifts the edges and the paint creeps underneath.
Cover the whole back panel, tape and all, then peel the tape off while the paint is still wet, corner first, pulling it back on itself. The number underneath stays white.
Clip the shirts on the line in the sun. August dries a t-shirt inside an hour.

August's handprint sheet while the shirts dry. Kreston goes first, while he is calm, with the wet washcloth already in your other hand. Then Azlyn goes on the same sheet beside him. Paint her palm with the brush rather than dipping her hand. Press flat, count to three, lift straight up. Write August, her 3 and his 14 months beside the pair in marker. If August is a month you want on the door frame, take both marks in pencil while they are standing still, with the name and the date beside each.
second.tip: Do a spare pillowcase first if you have one. The first number teaches you how much paint a sponge holds.

alternatives: Paper numbers only, taped to her front.
A painted hand on the shirt front instead of a number.
Paint the numbers on freehand and skip the tape.
Sort the morning's painted sheets into two piles by color.
outAgain: The museum, first Saturday of the month, and cool inside on the hottest afternoon of the week
The shady side of the park with Friday's ball
A friend's garden, and the shirts left drying
The library, for anything with a team in it
The paddling pool at home, if the line is out of the door
days.krestonPM: He walks the museum at 14 months, which means one gallery rather than four. Put him down where the floor is open and let him cover it on his own feet, then get him back in the stroller. Give him his own board book to hold on the way in.

insight.headline: Oil and water is the same lesson as the wax crayon and the sticker resist.
paras: Azlyn met one idea three times today in three materials. Oil sitting back up on top of the water, wax turning the paint away, tape holding a white number under a loaded sponge. The rule underneath all three is that some things refuse to mix, and the one doing the refusing wins. A three-year-old does not carry a rule from a single demonstration over to a new material on her own. She needs it in enough different clothes to strip out whatever was incidental about the first one. That is why the jar at breakfast earns its five minutes, and why the shirts matter.

days.safety: Use a plastic bottle for the shake rather than a glass jar, or keep your hand round the jar while she shakes it. The wax crayon and the candle stub are both choking size, so count them into a tin and stand it up high the moment the painting is done. Washable non-toxic paint only, because a 14-month-old gets a hand in it. Both children go out to the shed wall covered: hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. Pegs go back on the line at the end rather than down on the paving.

days.title: Somebody Has to Say Go
days.prepTonight: Hang the whistle on the back of the kitchen door, clear the hallway, and cut two arm-lengths of string for this afternoon.

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: Stop and Go Through the Sprinkler

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: The Bread and Butter on the Table

opening.title: One Blast, Two Blasts, Three
steps: Sit her at the table with the whistle between you. Blow it once. Then twice. Then three times.
Set the meanings out loud. One blast stop, two turn round, three everybody down on the floor. Have her say them back in order.
Practice sitting down. One blast and she freezes in her chair, three and she slides onto the floor. Then drop a cushion at each end of the hall.

main.title: Statues on the Whistle
materials: 1 whistle (a saucepan lid and a wooden spoon, or your own voice, does the same job)
1 roll masking tape for the start and finish lines
A clear hallway, or the coolest room in the house
steps: Tape a start line and a finish line at each end of the hallway and stand a cushion past each. Those are the turns.
Music on, and send her line to line however she wants to travel. Running, crawling, sideways, hopping.
One blast. She holds whatever shape she is in, mid-stride, until the next blast. Count three out loud while she wobbles, then let her go.
Add the second signal. Two blasts, she turns at the nearest cushion and comes back. Give her four or five before the third arrives.
Three blasts, everybody on the floor including you. Getting down there yourself is what makes her drop fast.
Hand her the whistle for the last ten minutes and run when she says run. She holds the stop for an unreasonable length of time.
main.tip: Blow the stop when she is going flat out, not when she is slowing down anyway.

outside.title: Stop and Go Through the Sprinkler
paras: Set the sprinkler on the grass and run the same three signals through it. One blast and she freezes in the spray. Two and she goes back through it the other way. Get out before eleven while the grass is cool underfoot, and take the whistle with you.

days.infant: Kreston is 14 months and will not freeze for anybody, so give him the edge of the spray rather than the middle. Sit him where the water arrives as mist and let him decide whether to walk in. He will work out that the water comes round again.

second.title: The Peg Scoreboard
second.intro: The rest of the week needs somewhere to put its points. It gets built once, sitting down, and used on three more days.
materials: 1 sheet of thick card, or a flattened box
String or thick wool, 2 arm-lengths, cut last night
Stickers or bottle caps for the point markers
steps: Lay the card flat and rule a line down the middle. Two teams. She names both and writes what she can of the names at the top.
Tape one string across the upper half, the other across the lower half. Pull each tight before the second tape goes down, or the clothespins sag instead of sliding.
Mark ten spaces under each string. Nought at the left, then a line for every point up to ten. She does the marks under the second string.
Clip a peg to the left end of each string. That is nought all, and a point moves a peg one space right.
Stick a sticker at the five and the ten on both strings, or tape a bottle cap there, so she finds halfway without counting.
Test it. Three points to you, four to her, one space at a time and counting out loud, then slide both back.
Stand it against the wall where it lives all week, spare pegs clipped along the top edge.
second.tip: Let her move both pegs, yours as well as hers, counting out loud.

alternatives: Two paper cups and dry pasta. One piece in for every point.
Chalk the score on the paving and start again each game.
Pegs along the clothesline, no card at all.
outAgain: Feeding the ducks, late enough that the pond has gone into shade
A long walk with the stroller and the whistle, one blast for stop at every curb
The playground, once the equipment has cooled enough to touch
A sunset walk after dinner instead, and skip this hour
days.krestonPM: Clip two of the spare pegs to the edge of the card for him and let him pull them off. At 14 months that pinch grip is work. At the pond he goes in the stroller or on your hip.

insight.headline: Freezing on cue is one of the best self-control exercises there is.
paras: Stopping a body that is already moving is one of the hardest things a three-year-old brain does. Azlyn has to hold a rule, catch a signal, and shut down a movement her legs have committed to. Researchers who study executive function use games close to this one as a measure, and how children handle them at four tracks with how they settle into a classroom later. The two-blast turn is a step up again, because it swaps one rule for another mid-run. She will fail the first few, and those are the ones doing the work. Every failed stop is practice, and the laughing is what keeps her doing thirty of them.

days.safety: A whistle is the exact size Kreston chokes on, and the pea inside it comes loose. It goes round your neck or in a high drawer, never on the floor. Keep him out of the running lane. At 14 months he walks straight into the path of a sprinting three-year-old. Wet skin burns quicker than dry, so both of them go into the sprinkler covered: hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

days.title: The Pitch on the Path
days.prepTonight: Flatten a cereal box and cut a dozen cards out of it, and stand the chalk, the crayons and an empty shoebox on the table beside them.

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: Chalking the Five Stations Onto the Path

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: The Cold Water Pitcher for Dinner

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Cool Bath, Then the Course Cards Again

opening.title: Walking the Edges
opening.need: her shoes · 1 piece of chalk · the path or the drive.
steps: Shoes on, out before the paving warms, and walk the path end to end counting steps out loud.
Walk it again down one edge and back down the other.
Chalk a cross at each end. That is the pitch, and everything she picks at nine has to fit between the two crosses.

main.title: The Five That Made It
materials: 10–12 cards cut from a cereal box
Crayons for her to draw each event
1 shoebox with a lid, for the ones that do not make it
This morning's two chalk crosses on the path
steps: Sit down with the cards and ask what she wants in her games. Running, jumping, throwing, hopping, the dog joining in. Write each on its own card in her words.
She colors each card while you write the next. Ten or twelve, then stop, even if she has more.
Take the cards and the tape out to the path. Lay them between this morning's two crosses, one per station, with running room between them.
They will not all fit. Five is what the path holds. Say it straight and hand the decision to her. Five stay, the rest go in the shoebox.
Do not rescue the ones she cuts. She drops them in herself, and you write RESERVES on the lid so nothing is gone for good.
Tape the five survivors down in order and read them out end to end. That is her program.
main.tip: Resist steering her five towards the ones that will work. Her list will include something impossible, and the path tells her so.

outside.title: Chalking the Five Stations Onto the Path
paras: Straight on from the table with the chalk. Draw a station round every taped card: a start line, a box to jump out of, a circle to throw into. Work the shaded end first and move down as the sun comes round. Shoes stay on, and the water bottle stands in the shade.

days.infant: Kreston is 14 months and scribbling, so give him a fat piece of chalk at the shaded end and his own square of paving. He drags it, drops it and eats some of the dust, which is why it is chalk and not marker. Sit him where he can watch Azlyn run the line.

second.title: The Same Course, Teddy Sized
second.intro: The path is too hot to kneel on by one o'clock, so the course comes indoors at teddy scale. Everything shrinks except the number of stations.
materials: 1 large tray, or a flattened box, as the base
1 foil ball or 1 ping-pong ball (no marbles)
Her five event cards from this morning
steps: Peel the five cards off the path on the way in and lay them along one edge of the tray in order. The tray is the pitch now.
Draw the lines onto the tray with the marker. A start, a finish, and whatever the middle three need.
Build the equipment from what is on the table. Two cups on their sides make a goal, two straws taped across two upright cups make a hurdle, a cardboard scrap folded double stands up as a wall.
Tape every piece down.
Put the ball at the start line and check it fits through the cup goal. Squash the foil ball smaller if it will not go, or swap it for something that fits.
Run the first teddy through all five stations with her holding it, in card order.
Leave her to run the other teddies on her own, and let her decide what the winner gets.
second.tip: Animate the teddy rather than sliding it. She narrates a toy that moves its own legs.

alternatives: One cup, one ball, and a teddy that shoots from further back each time.
Draw the course on paper instead of building it.
Run the five stations indoors at her own size, down the hallway.
outAgain: The hill walk, up at half past two under the trees, with a stop at the top
The riverside path, shaded all afternoon
The paddling pool, if the hill is more than either of you has in you
The green space with Friday's ball
days.krestonPM: Give him one teddy and one paper cup of his own on the floor beside the tray. At 14 months he puts a thing into a container and takes it out again. On the hill he walks the flat bit at the top.

insight.headline: Choosing what to leave out is harder than choosing what to include.
paras: Azlyn can name ten things she wants in forty seconds. Asking which five to drop is a different job, because every card that goes in the box is something she gives up while holding the reason in her head. Three-year-olds manage the dropping far better when the limit comes from the world instead of from you. The path is five stations long, a fact she can walk the length of, so the argument is with the path. The reserve box matters as much as the limit does, because nothing she drops is thrown away. She is ordering the cards rather than destroying any of them, and that is what keeps her deciding instead of digging in.

days.safety: August paving gets hot enough to burn bare feet by mid-morning. Shoes on, chalk at the shaded end, and a water bottle out there with you. Hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven, because an hour of chalking on an open path is an hour of full sun. Both children come in the moment either goes red-faced. The foil ball and the ping-pong ball are both small enough for Kreston to swallow, so whichever one she uses stays on the tray and off the floor.

days.title: Jumping Into Sand
days.prepTonight: Tip the play sand into the large shallow tub tonight, stand a pitcher of water beside it, and put the swimming bag by the front door.

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Sand Tray on the Back Step

opening.title: Raking the Sand Flat
opening.need: the tray of sand · 1 pitcher of water · her two hands.
steps: Walk her fingers through the dry sand, then pour half the pitcher over one end while she stirs.
Press your flat hand into the damp end, then the dry end. Damp sand keeps the print and dry sand fills it in.
Sweep the tray level with the side of her forearm and smooth it with her palms. She resets it after every jump.

main.title: Where Her Heels Land
materials: 1 bag of washed play sand in a large shallow storage tub or the paddling pool (a tray of potting soil does the same job)
Craft sticks or clothespins, 3, to mark each landing
1 pitcher of water for damping the sand
steps: Chalk a take-off line on the paving at the edge of the tray. Her toes go behind it.
First jump: arms at her sides, no run-up. Push a craft stick in behind the dent her heels leave.
Cut a string from the chalk line to the stick. Write ONE on the stick and tie the string round it.
Smooth the sand, damp it from the pitcher if it has gone crumbly, and jump again with her arms swinging. Mark it, cut a second string, label that stick TWO.
Hold the two strings side by side. The arms one is longer.
Last jump: she wades to the far end through the sand and goes from in there. Her legs will not do what they did on the paving. Cut a third string, label it THREE, and lay all three in order.
main.tip: Measure to the heels and say so out loud every time. Three-year-olds measure to whichever bit went furthest.

outside.title: Jumping the Widening River
paras: Chalk two lines on the paving a hand's width apart and call the gap a river. She jumps it, you widen it by a hand, she jumps again. Keep going until she lands in the water, then go back two hands and let her clear it three times. Work the shaded side of the house, and let her watch you miss it too.

days.infant: Kreston is 14 months and nowhere near jumping, since both feet leaving the ground is closer to two. He has bend and spring, so hold both his hands and let him bounce on the spot at the edge of the chalk.

second.title: Everybody's Jump on the Wall
second.intro: Indoors the floor is cool and the measuring carries on, with everybody in the house on the line.
materials: A clear wall, or the back of a door
steps: Tape a take-off line across the hall floor. Everyone jumps from behind it, standing start, no run-up.
Azlyn goes first. Mark where her heels land with tape and write her name on it.
Take your turn, then anyone else home, each with a taped and named mark.
Cut a string for every jump, floor line to landing mark, and wrap tape round one end as a label with the name on it.
Hang the strings on the wall side by side, all from the same height, and let her sort them longest to shortest before you tape anything down.
Ask her who went furthest and why. Take the answer as it comes. Legs turn up in it somewhere.
Leave them up. Anybody who visits gets a jump and a string.
second.tip: Do not shorten your own jump to keep it close to hers. She reads a wall of strings as a fact about grown legs.

alternatives: Tape marks on the floor only. Skip the strings and the wall.
Jump off the bottom stair and compare it with the standing jump.
Frog, rabbit and kangaroo jumps down the hall, no measuring.
outAgain: Swimming, the weekly hour and the best place in town in August
The splash pad, if the session is booked out
The paddling pool with the sprinkler going
A shaded walk and a popsicle, if nobody can face chlorine
days.krestonPM: He comes to the pool. At 14 months he walks the shallow end holding both your hands, so let him wade rather than float. Twenty-five minutes, then out and warm before he goes quiet on you.

insight.headline: Sand is one of the best materials there is, and it's the resistance that makes it good.
paras: Sand answers back in proportion. Press hard and it holds the print, press soft and it does nothing, wade through it and her legs have to find more than they needed on the paving. It also has no correct outcome, so she cannot get it wrong and cannot finish it, and she stays with a tray of it long after she abandons a puzzle. Damp sand and dry sand behave like two different substances, and moving between them is her first real handle on why water changes things. Sand is patient with a three-year-old's hands and still makes her work for what she wants, which is why twenty minutes in it outlasts twenty minutes at almost anything else.

days.safety: Use washed play sand, not construction sand. Kreston will put it in his mouth and rub it into his eyes at 14 months, so he gets a dishwashing bowl of his own sand, set well clear of the landing end, and you stay close enough to touch him. Azlyn comes down heels first into the big tray, so keep him out of it. Tip any standing water out of the tray before either child gets near it. He stays within arm's reach at the pool as well. A morning on open paving is a morning in full sun: hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. The scissors stay with you.

days.prepTonight: Fill the ice tray, stand the thawed juice concentrate and six clear cups by the water pitcher, and rinse ten bottle caps to dry.

opening.title: The Oranges Cut Into Smiles
opening.need: 2 oranges · 1 board · 1 sharp knife (adult only) · 1 plate.
steps: Cut both oranges into six wedges on the board, then put the knife away before she sits down.
Show her the trick. Bite the flesh out from inside and the peel left in your mouth is a wide orange grin. Do yours first.
Two wedges each now. The rest go on the plate in the fridge for half time, and she carries them out.

main.title: Too Strong, Too Weak, Just Right
materials: Frozen juice concentrate, thawed, or lemon juice and sugar
1 tray to carry it all out on
steps: Line three of the clear cups up. She pours the same amount of cold water into each from the pitcher.
Cup one gets four tablespoons of concentrate. Cup two gets one teaspoon. Say the numbers out loud as they go in and let her stir both.
She tastes cup one, then cup two. Take the face she makes as the result and give her the words. Too strong. Too weak.
Cup three is hers. She adds concentrate a teaspoon at a time, tastes after every one, and stops when she says stop. Count the spoons out loud and let her number stand.
Write her recipe on the card in her own measurements. Her spoons, that cup, that much water.
Make the last three cups to her card, drop the ice in and load the tray.
main.tip: No concentrate in the house works fine. Lemon juice and a spoon of sugar give her two things to adjust instead of one.

outside.title: Carrying the Cold Drinks to the Shady Bench
paras: She carries the tray. Pick the bench you can see from the gate and walk it at her pace with the cups sliding about. Drink them out there rather than at the table. The green stripes in the grass show where the shade sits.

days.infant: Kreston is 14 months and drinks from an open cup with two hands if you fill it a third full. Give him a little of the juice he watched her mix and let him hold it himself. On the walk he would rather push the stroller than ride in it, so allow ten spare minutes.

second.title: The Bottle Cap Cup
second.intro: A whole tournament fits on a table top, with everybody sitting down.
materials: 1 shoebox lid, or a sheet of thick card
1 paper cup, or a matchbox, as the goal
1 small box with a lid, for counting the caps back into
steps: Tape the shoebox lid flat to the table, open side up.
Lay the paper cup on its side at the far end and tape it down. That is the goal.
Mark every cap. Five for her team, five for yours, and she decides what the two marks mean.
Show her the flick. One finger held back against the thumb and let go, not a push and not a throw. The first ten go on the floor.
Take turns. A cap in the cup is a point, a cap off the lid loses the turn.
After every point she walks to the peg scoreboard from Sunday and moves the peg one space.
Play to five, swap ends and play again. Count the caps into the small box at the end.
second.tip: Start her a hand's width from the goal rather than at the far end. A three-year-old who scores in the first two minutes stays at the table for twenty.

alternatives: Flick the caps at a chalk target instead of into a goal.
Sort the caps by color and by size and stop there.
Build a tower of caps and count how many before it goes over.
outAgain: Indoor playground, the quiet session, and the coolest hour available indoors
The library on the way home, for anything with a ball on the cover
A friend's house with the paddling pool out
The garden and the hose, if leaving is beyond everybody
days.krestonPM: He is not at this table. Bottle caps go in the mouth inside four seconds at 14 months, so set him up on the floor with the empty pitcher and the tablespoon. At indoor playground he gets the under-twos area on his own feet.

insight.headline: "Too much" and "not enough" is a real concept, and it's rarely taught.
paras: Azlyn knows more and less. Both are easy, because you can see them. Too much needs a target, and that target sits in her own mouth rather than in the cup. Taste, add a spoon, taste again is the whole method for cooking, for mixing paint, for how hard to throw a ball, and she gets almost no practice at it. She adjusts, checks, adjusts again and lands on an answer nobody handed her. Her number will come out sweeter than yours, and the card is a record of what she decided rather than what you would have poured. Write it as it stands.

days.safety: Bottle caps are the classic choking size and there will be ten of them on a table Kreston can reach standing up. Play where he cannot get to them, count them into the box at the end, and put the box up high. He never gets one to hold, however hard he asks; a jar lid too wide for his mouth is the swap. The walk to the bench runs in open sun, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. The orange knife goes back in the drawer before either child is at the table.

days.prepTonight: Put two blank cards and the marker on the table, and stand the cup, the kitchen foil and a piece of thick card beside them for the trophy.

opening.title: Her Rules for Hide and Seek
steps: Play one round her way and correct nothing, including a count to ten with four numbers in it.
Ask her for the rules afterwards and write each on the card as it comes. Where you can hide, when you can look, what happens once you are found.
Read the card back. She changes two of them on the spot.

main.title: The Game Nobody Has Played Before
materials: The ball she wound on Friday, or any ball
Chalk, or masking tape, for the lines
Paper cups, clothespins and whatever else she names as equipment
steps: Sit her down with the ball, the cushions, the cups and the clothespins in a heap and ask her to make up a game. Then say nothing for a full minute.
Write her rules onto the first card word for word. Do not tidy them, and do not ask the questions she has not thought of yet.
Chalk or tape the lines she names and leave the cushions where she puts them, including the one behind the sofa.
Play it as written, including the parts that fall apart. If something breaks, ask her for the rule rather than offering one, and write it under the old.
Play the mended version twice more. She amends it again.
Read the card back and let her name the game. Write the name across the second card and copy the final rules onto it in order.
main.tip: Play to lose the first round. She writes fairer rules for a game she has already won.

outside.title: Playing It Again in the Shade
paras: Take the card, the ball and two cushions down the shaded side of the house and run the game outdoors. More space changes it and she will amend the rules again inside five minutes. Get somebody else into it if there is anyone about, so she has to explain it.

days.infant: Kreston is 14 months, has three to five words you can make out, and one of them gets used on the ball this week. Put him in the game with a job of his own. He stands at one cushion and Azlyn brings the ball to him.

second.title: The Trophy Made Out of a Cup
second.intro: Everything this week has been building towards somebody holding something up.
materials: 1 piece of thick card for the base
The chalked course, the peg scoreboard, the numbered shirts and the whistle from this week
steps: Turn the cup upside down and tape it to the middle of the card base with packing tape, right round the rim. It has to survive being waved about.
Tear a long strip of foil and wind it round the cup, shiny side out, while she smooths it with her thumbs. Two layers, masking tape underneath where it will not show.
Roll two short strips of foil into ropes and tape one to each side as handles.
Write the name of her game across the base, leaving room underneath.

Set the course up outside in the shade. If Monday's five chalked stations are in full sun by now, chalk them again down the shaded side of the house. The scoreboard goes against the wall, the whistle round your neck, and a numbered shirt on everybody who is home.
Run all five events end to end, one blast for stop between each, a peg moved for every point.
Whoever wins holds the trophy over their head. Then write every player's name round the base and stand it on the shelf.
second.tip: All the names on the base, in the order they finished and in the same size letters. A trophy that records only the winner gets played for once, then shelved.

alternatives: Foil round a cardboard tube, no cup and no base.
Medals instead: foil circles on wool, one per neck.
Run the five events with no trophy and hand out oranges instead.
outAgain: The pharmacy for the sun cream you have run through, then the bench outside
The park at the end of the road, trophy in her bag for whoever is there
Grandparents, if anybody wants the prize-giving again
The green space with the ball, one last game of hers
days.krestonPM: He gets a shirt as well, hanging past his knees, and a name on the base like everyone else. At 14 months he cannot run a course, so give him the last station and let Azlyn finish by handing him the ball. Outside the pharmacy he wants down and walking, so let him.

insight.headline: Asking for her rule is better than checking her answer.
paras: A rule broke this morning and you asked her what it should be, so she had to put the thinking into words rather than hand you a result. Children who explain their own reasoning hold onto it longer than children who hear whether they were right, and the effect turns up as young as three. Asking gives you the only view you get of what is going on in there. Her rule will sometimes be wrong and interesting at once, which is worth more than a correct answer, because you can see where it came from. She defends a game she wrote and abandons a game you fixed.

days.safety: The whistle is out on the grass again this afternoon. It goes round your neck between blasts and never down on the ground. It is the one object this week that is the exact size Kreston chokes on, and at 14 months he mouths whatever he finds at his own height. One o'clock is the hottest the day gets in August, so run the whole thing in shade, shoes on both children, and the water pitcher out there beside the scoreboard. Hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven, and again before the course starts. Both children come in the moment either goes red-faced.
